items.note: голова́: head. This letter is the h sound; the g sound has its own letter, ґ.
items.comment: Judgement call: Ukrainian г is voiced [ɦ] (Wikipedia, Wiktionary IPA for голова́), so English h in hat is an approximation. It is the same comparison Wikipedia makes (h in hello) and is acceptable.

items.note: ґа́нок: porch. A rare letter, but easy to confuse with г.

items.comment: Goroh's entry and Wiktionary both give йо́гурт. A reader comment on the Goroh page cites Ponomariv for two accepted stresses (йо́гурт and йогу́рт); I could not confirm that second stress in a dictionary. The stress shown is valid either way.
Wiktionary glosses кіт as male cat or tomcat, with кішка as the female. "cat" is acceptable as a simple gloss.
Judgement call: Wikipedia compares о /ɔ/ to the o in long; port is a comparable vowel but is long and, for rhotic speakers, followed by r. Acceptable as an approximation.
Wiktionary glosses пес as male dog, with собака as a synonym. "dog" is acceptable.
рука́ means both hand and arm (Wiktionary). "hand" is correct but only part of the meaning; acceptable for an example word.

items.comment: Wiktionary treats дідусь as the diminutive or affectionate form of дід, which is closer to "grandpa" but also used as the everyday word. "grandfather" is acceptable.

Example verified: Goroh and English Wiktionary's Ukrainian section both give авто́бус, masculine, "bus". The а in this example is unstressed (Wiktionary IPA [ɐu̯ˈtɔbʊs]), so it shows the letter but is not the clearest model of the father vowel; that does not make the cell wrong.

items.note: вода́: water. Often softer than an English v, and like w at the end of a syllable, as in був (was).
items.comment: Note verified: був is the masculine past of бути, "was" (Goroh, Wiktionary), with IPA [buu̯] (Wiktionary) and /buu̯/ (Wikipedia, Ukrainian phonology). Wikipedia and Ukrainian Wikipedia both describe в as [w]/[u̯] after a vowel in the syllable coda, so "like w at the end of a syllable" is correct. Judgement call on the unchanged clue: "v, as in van" remains a simplification, and Wiktionary transcribes the example itself as [wɔˈda], so the w-like sound is not limited to syllable ends. "Often softer than an English v" covers this loosely, and I accept the clue and note together. "was" is masculine only; a woman says була́.

items.note: ри́ба: fish. Like the i in bit, never the ee sound, which is і.
items.comment: Note verified: Wiktionary gives ри́ба [ˈrɪbɐ], "fish", and Wikipedia gives и as /ɪ/. "never the ee sound" is not contradicted by the sources I read: English and Ukrainian Wikipedia describe unstressed и as moving toward е, not toward і. Ukrainian Wikipedia's И article says the letter renders [і] in borrowed common nouns; I read this as the spelling of foreign [i] in loanwords, not as a statement that и is pronounced ee, but the fetched text does not settle that. The note leaves out the unstressed drift toward е, which is an acceptable simplification.

Goroh gives ону́ка (animate, feminine, 1st declension). English Wiktionary gives ону́ка [oˈnukɐ], "granddaughter", with вну́ка as an alternative form. Goroh's definition page and slovnyk.ua (СУМ) cross-refer онука to внука, defined on Goroh as "Дочка сина або дочки". Standard Ukrainian and not a Russian form; unlike онучка, it showed no foot-wrap homonym in the entries I read.
